note: Ordered curriculum graph for a Thinking-Method tutor (English speaker learning French). Each node is a scaffold, not a script: the tutor uses these fields to run a live Socratic exchange. prereqs list node ids that must be mastered before a node unlocks. Nodes c01-c12 are the original hand-checked core; c13+ are machine-authored in the same spirit and pending fluent-speaker verification. Built in the spirit of the method, not copied from any course.

constructions.title: The words you already own
constructions.goal: Feel the head start: thousands of French words are already yours.
constructions.transferHook: English '-tion' nouns are spelled the same in French (information, nation, situation, direction); '-able/-ible' and '-ent/-ant' words too (possible, important, différent). Only the pronunciation changes.
constructions.targetPattern: Recognize and attempt to pronounce cognate nouns and adjectives.
constructions.watchFor: This node is about realization and pronunciation, not making sentences yet. The win is the learner feeling how much they already have.

constructions.title: It is → c'est
constructions.goal: Make a first real French sentence using the cognates.
constructions.transferHook: 'c'est' ≈ 'it's / that's / this is'. Bolt it onto a word they already own.
constructions.watchFor: Keep it to c'est + one word at first. Let them build up, don't hand them long sentences.

constructions.title: It's not → c'est pas
constructions.goal: Negate what they can already say.
constructions.transferHook: 'pas' ≈ 'not'. Formally French wraps the verb (ne ... pas), but in speech people drop the 'ne': 'c'est pas possible'.
constructions.targetPattern: c'est pas + X   (formal: ce n'est pas + X)
constructions.watchFor: Let them discover where 'pas' sits. Introduce the full ne...pas only after the spoken form lands.

constructions.title: I want to → je veux + verb
constructions.goal: Unlock generative speech: want + a huge set of cognate verbs.
constructions.transferHook: Many French verbs end in '-er' and are cousins of English ones: préparer, organiser, continuer, décider, arriver. 'je veux' ≈ 'I want'.
constructions.watchFor: This is the big unlock — let them feel that one pattern + many cognate verbs = many sentences.

constructions.title: There is no 'to'
constructions.goal: Internalize a key structural contrast with English.
constructions.transferHook: English says 'I want TO continue'; French just says 'je veux continuer' — nothing stands in for 'to'.
constructions.targetPattern: Reinforce c04 with no inserted word between veux and the verb.
constructions.watchFor: The classic beginner error is inserting 'à' or a word for 'to'. Guide them to leave the gap empty; don't just correct it.

constructions.title: I can → je peux + verb
constructions.goal: Reuse the modal-plus-verb machine with a new modal.
constructions.transferHook: 'je peux' ≈ 'I can'. Same shape as 'je veux': modal + bare infinitive.
constructions.watchFor: Same no-'to' rule as c05. Let them notice the pattern is identical.

constructions.title: I'm going to → je vais + verb
constructions.goal: Get the near future for free.
constructions.transferHook: French uses 'aller' (to go) + a verb exactly like English 'going to': 'je vais préparer' = 'I'm going to prepare'.
constructions.watchFor: Distinguish from literal 'I go to a place'. Here it's future, same as English 'going to'.

constructions.title: Asking, the easy way
constructions.goal: Turn any statement into a question with no new grammar.
constructions.transferHook: Easiest question = say the statement with a rising tone, or put 'est-ce que' in front.
constructions.watchFor: Do not introduce inversion yet. Keep it to intonation and est-ce que.

constructions.title: Changing the doer → tu, on
constructions.goal: Swap the subject with minimal conjugation.
constructions.transferHook: 'je veux' → 'tu veux' (you) → 'on peut' (we, in speech). Small, controlled steps.
constructions.watchFor: Introduce one subject at a time. Don't dump a conjugation table.

constructions.title: Do it → le faire
constructions.goal: Meet a structural contrast: the pronoun comes before the verb.
constructions.transferHook: English 'do it' puts 'it' after. French 'le faire' puts it before: 'je veux le faire' = 'I want to do it'.
constructions.watchFor: The word order flip is the whole lesson. Let them place the pronoun themselves and feel where it goes.

constructions.title: Gluing sentences → mais, parce que, avec
constructions.goal: Extend sentences cheaply and sound more fluent.
constructions.transferHook: 'mais' (but), 'parce que' (because), 'avec' (with) let them chain what they can already say.
examples: je veux continuer mais c'est difficile
je peux le faire parce que c'est possible
constructions.watchFor: Reward longer sentences built only from pieces they already own.

constructions.title: The past → j'ai + verb-é
constructions.goal: Say what they did, using the same cognate verbs.
constructions.transferHook: 'j'ai' = 'I have'; '-er' verbs become '-é'. So 'j'ai préparé' ≈ 'I have prepared / I prepared'. Mirrors English 'have + -ed'.
constructions.watchFor: Two things land here (j'ai + the -é ending). Introduce the -é first, then attach j'ai. One step at a time.

constructions.title: You have to → il faut + verb
constructions.goal: Express necessity with one frozen chunk plus any infinitive.
constructions.transferHook: 'il faut' is one unchanging chunk ≈ 'it's necessary / you have to'. Same modal machine as je veux/je peux: chunk + bare infinitive, no 'to'.
constructions.watchFor: Learners try to conjugate it or add a subject like 'tu'. It never changes — that's the gift.

constructions.title: I'd like → je voudrais
constructions.goal: Sound polite with a single new form of a known verb.
constructions.transferHook: English softens 'I want' to 'I'd like'; French softens 'je veux' to 'je voudrais'. Same slot, same no-'to' rule.
constructions.watchFor: Don't explain the conditional yet — treat 'je voudrais' as a polite chunk. The system comes later (c44).

constructions.title: The formal not → ne ... pas
constructions.goal: Upgrade spoken negation to the written/formal sandwich.
constructions.transferHook: They already use 'pas' (c03). Writing and careful speech wrap the verb: 'je ne veux pas'. English has nothing like the sandwich — feel it as a frame around the verb.
constructions.watchFor: Before a vowel 'ne' becomes n' (n'est). Let them hear that it's the same sentence they already say, dressed up.

constructions.title: I like → j'aime + verb or noun
constructions.goal: Talk about likes with one verb and everything they own.
constructions.transferHook: 'j'aime' ≈ 'I like/love'. Like English, it takes a verb ('I like to organize') or a noun — but with no 'to': 'j'aime organiser'.
constructions.watchFor: With nouns French demands le/la/les where English drops the article ('I like coffee' → 'j'aime LE café'). Let them discover the needed article.

constructions.title: I must → je dois + verb
constructions.goal: Complete the modal family: want, can, must.
constructions.transferHook: 'je dois' ≈ 'I must / I have to'. Third member of the modal machine — identical shape to je veux and je peux.
constructions.watchFor: Contrast with 'il faut' (impersonal) — 'je dois' is personal. Let them feel the difference by asking who has to do it.

constructions.title: He wants, she can → il veut, elle peut
constructions.goal: Talk about other people with tiny sound changes.
constructions.transferHook: je veux → il/elle veut, je peux → il/elle peut: the written ending changes but the SOUND barely does. French conjugation is easier on the ear than on the page.
constructions.targetPattern: il / elle + veut / peut / va / doit + [infinitive]
constructions.watchFor: One subject at a time, sound first, spelling second. Don't open a conjugation table.

constructions.title: We and formal you → nous, vous
constructions.goal: Complete the persons: nous ...-ons, vous ...-ez.
constructions.transferHook: Two reliable machine rules: nous → verb ends in '-ons' (nous allons), vous → '-ez' (vous voulez). 'vous' doubles as the polite 'you' — like addressing someone as 'Sir'.
constructions.watchFor: Speech prefers 'on' for we (they know it from c09) — nous is for writing and emphasis. Teach vous as the stranger-safe you.

constructions.title: What → qu'est-ce que
constructions.goal: Ask open 'what' questions with one memorized key.
constructions.transferHook: 'qu'est-ce que' is a frozen chunk ≈ 'what'. Sounds like 'kess-kuh'. Then attach any statement they already own: 'qu'est-ce que tu veux ?'
constructions.watchFor: Don't dissect the chunk's inner grammar — it's a key, not a sentence. 'qu'est-ce que c'est ?' = 'what is it?' is worth memorizing whole.

constructions.title: Why / because → pourquoi / parce que
constructions.goal: Ask for reasons and give them.
constructions.transferHook: 'pourquoi ?' ≈ 'why?', and they already own 'parce que' (c11). Question and answer form a natural pair.
constructions.watchFor: Spoken French happily says 'pourquoi tu veux...' without inversion. Keep it conversational.

constructions.title: Where and when → où, quand
constructions.goal: Complete the everyday question words.
constructions.transferHook: 'où' (where) and 'quand' (when) drop into the same slot as pourquoi: question word + the statement they already own.
examples: quand est-ce que tu veux commencer ?
constructions.watchFor: 'où' vs 'ou' (or) differ by one accent — flag it lightly when writing, ignore in speech.

constructions.title: There is / there are → il y a
constructions.goal: Describe what exists with one all-purpose chunk.
constructions.transferHook: 'il y a' is one frozen chunk ≈ 'there is / there are' — no singular/plural change, unlike English.
constructions.targetPattern: il y a + [noun]  /  il n'y a pas de + [noun]
examples: il n'y a pas de problème
constructions.watchFor: The negative flips the article to 'de' ('pas de problème'). Let them meet that as a fixed pattern, not a rule lecture.

constructions.title: Un/une and the shape of adjectives
constructions.goal: Meet gender agreement without fear: articles first, endings second.
constructions.transferHook: English has 'a'; French splits it: un/une. Many adjectives just add an 'e' for feminine — often changing only the sound's ending (important → importante: the 't' wakes up).
constructions.watchFor: Don't demand memorized genders — give the noun's gender away free and let them shape the adjective. Sound the final consonant appearing.

constructions.title: Done, said, seen → fait, dit, vu
constructions.goal: Extend the past to the most common irregular participles.
constructions.transferHook: English also has irregular pasts (do→done, say→said, see→seen). French's big three: fait (done), dit (said), vu (seen) — short, punchy, everywhere.
constructions.watchFor: Only these few forms — resist listing more. Each is a single syllable to own for life.

constructions.title: I went → je suis allé
constructions.goal: Meet the second past auxiliary: movement verbs take être.
constructions.transferHook: Old English did this too ('he is come'). A small club of going/coming verbs uses 'je suis' instead of 'j'ai': je suis allé (I went), je suis arrivé, je suis parti.
constructions.targetPattern: je suis + allé / arrivé / parti / venu
constructions.watchFor: Keep the club tiny (aller, arriver, partir, venir). Agreement (-e, -s) is a spelling matter — mention only if they write.

constructions.title: It was → c'était
constructions.goal: Describe the past (background) versus events.
constructions.transferHook: They own 'c'est'; the past-description version is 'c'était' ≈ 'it was'. Pair: 'c'était difficile, mais j'ai continué' — was-ness vs happened-ness, just like English.
constructions.watchFor: Don't teach the imparfait system — just these two chunks (c'était, il y avait) as past scenery.

constructions.title: My, your → mon/ma, ton/ta
constructions.goal: Claim things: possessives that agree with the thing, not the owner.
constructions.transferHook: Key flip from English: 'sa décision' can be his OR her decision — the word matches the NOUN's gender, not the owner's. mon/ma/mes work like a/une: mon projet, ma situation.
constructions.watchFor: The owner-vs-thing flip is the entire lesson. Test it with 'his decision' → 'sa décision'.

constructions.title: This, that → ce, cette, ces
constructions.goal: Point at things with the ce family.
constructions.transferHook: They already say 'c'est' — 'ce' is hiding inside it. ce projet (masc), cette situation (fem), ces idées (plural): one word, three shapes, same job as this/that.
constructions.watchFor: French doesn't split this/that — 'ce' covers both. Don't let them hunt for a 'that' word.

constructions.title: Me and you before the verb → me, te
constructions.goal: Extend the pronoun-first rule from things to people.
constructions.transferHook: Same flip they met in 'le faire' (c10): 'tu ME comprends' = 'you understand ME' — the me jumps in front of the verb.
constructions.watchFor: Word order is the whole lesson again. Build from 'tu comprends' → insert 'me'.

constructions.title: There → y (j'y vais)
constructions.goal: Replace places with one letter.
constructions.transferHook: 'y' ≈ 'there', and like all French pronouns it goes BEFORE the verb: 'j'y vais' = 'I'm going (there)'. English drops 'there'; French insists on the little y.
constructions.watchFor: 'on y va' is the everyday 'let's go' — worth owning as a chunk. With modals the y sticks to the infinitive: 'je veux y aller'.

constructions.title: Some of it → en (j'en veux)
constructions.goal: Replace quantities with en.
constructions.transferHook: 'en' ≈ 'of it / some': 'j'en veux' = 'I want some'. English can drop it ('I want some'); French makes it a pre-verb pronoun like y and me.
constructions.watchFor: Keep to frozen high-value chunks (j'en veux, il y en a). The full en-replacement rule can wait.

constructions.title: Myself → je me prépare
constructions.goal: Meet reflexive verbs as the me-rule turned on oneself.
constructions.transferHook: They know 'me' before the verb (c30). Point it at yourself: 'je me prépare' = 'I get (myself) ready'. English hides the myself; French says it.
constructions.watchFor: 'je m'appelle' (my name is) is the flagship — let them decode it as 'I call myself'.

constructions.title: More ... than → plus ... que
constructions.goal: Compare anything with two little words.
constructions.transferHook: English needs '-er' or 'more'; French always uses 'plus': plus important que = more important than. One rule, no exceptions to start.
examples: elle est plus organisée que moi
constructions.watchFor: Warn gently that 'plus' here sounds 'plü' (the s sleeps). 'moins' = less gives them the other direction free.

constructions.title: A lot of → beaucoup de
constructions.goal: Quantify with the de-family.
constructions.transferHook: All French quantity words end in 'de': beaucoup de (a lot of), un peu de (a bit of), trop de (too much). The 'de' never changes — easier than English's much/many split.
constructions.watchFor: No article after de ('beaucoup de travail', never 'beaucoup du travail'). Let them hear the clean pattern.

constructions.title: Yesterday, today, tomorrow → hier, aujourd'hui, demain
constructions.goal: Anchor tenses to time words they can reuse everywhere.
constructions.transferHook: Three words unlock time-travel with grammar they own: hier + j'ai fait (past), aujourd'hui + je fais, demain + je vais faire (future). English works identically.
constructions.watchFor: This node is assembly, not new grammar — reward long correct sentences mixing tense and time word.

constructions.title: If you want → si tu veux
constructions.goal: Make offers and conditions with si + present.
constructions.transferHook: 'si' = 'if', and beginner French conditions use plain present on both sides: 'si tu veux, on peut continuer' — exactly like English 'if you want, we can continue'.
examples: si tu veux, on peut continuer
si c'est possible, je vais le faire
constructions.watchFor: 'si' + 'il' contracts to s'il (s'il te plaît hides here!). No conditional mood yet — present + present is fully correct.

constructions.title: The thing that I want → la chose que je veux
constructions.goal: Glue a mini-sentence onto a noun with que.
constructions.transferHook: English: 'the thing (that) I want' — that is optional. French 'que' is mandatory but works the same: 'la chose que je veux'. qui = who/that (subject side).
examples: c'est la chose que je veux
constructions.watchFor: 'ce que' = 'what' in the middle of a sentence ('c'est ce que je veux' = that's what I want) — a high-value chunk.

constructions.title: In the middle of → en train de
constructions.goal: Say what's happening right now.
constructions.transferHook: French has no -ing tense; instead a chunk: 'je suis en train de préparer' = 'I'm (in the middle of) preparing'. être + en train de + infinitive.
examples: je suis en train de travailler
elle est en train de décider
constructions.watchFor: Learners reach for a French '-ing'. There isn't one — plain present or en train de covers it.

constructions.title: Just did → je viens de + verb
constructions.goal: Get the just-happened past for free.
constructions.transferHook: 'je viens de finir' literally 'I come from finishing' = 'I just finished'. Like 'je vais + verb' gave the future, 'je viens de + verb' gives the fresh past.
constructions.targetPattern: je viens de / tu viens de + [infinitive]
constructions.watchFor: Mirror it against je vais + verb so they feel the symmetry: going-to future, coming-from past.

constructions.title: Commands → regarde, allons-y, dis-moi
constructions.goal: Give instructions by dropping the subject.
constructions.transferHook: Like English, French commands just drop the subject: 'tu regardes' → 'regarde !'. Bonus chunks: allons-y (let's go), dis-moi (tell me) — pronouns hop BEHIND in commands.
constructions.watchFor: The pronoun flip (dis-MOI vs tu ME dis) will surprise them — present it as commands being pushy: the verb goes first.

constructions.title: Never, nothing, anymore → jamais, rien, plus
constructions.goal: Swap pas for richer negatives in the same sandwich.
constructions.transferHook: The ne...pas frame they own accepts other fillings: ne...jamais (never), ne...rien (nothing), ne...plus (not anymore). Same slots, new meanings.
constructions.watchFor: 'plus' meaning 'no more' sounds 'plü' (silent s) — opposite of the 'more' plus. Sound is the disambiguator; flag it.

constructions.title: I've been ... for → depuis + present
constructions.goal: Express ongoing duration with a structural surprise.
constructions.transferHook: Big contrast: English says 'I HAVE BEEN working for two hours'; French uses plain PRESENT: 'je travaille depuis deux heures'. The situation continues, so French stays in the present.
constructions.watchFor: The classic error is importing the perfect tense ('j'ai travaillé depuis...'). Walk them to why present makes sense: it's still true now.

constructions.title: Would → je voudrais, ce serait, je ferais
constructions.goal: Open the would-world from the voudrais they already own.
constructions.transferHook: They've said 'je voudrais' since c14. The '-rais' ending IS would: ce serait (it would be), je ferais (I would do), j'aimerais (I would like). One sound, whole mood.
constructions.watchFor: Grow it from known chunks, not conjugation tables. 'ce serait + adjective' is the workhorse.

constructions.title: I think that → je pense que
constructions.goal: Wrap any owned sentence in an opinion.
constructions.transferHook: 'je pense que' = 'I think that', and unlike English the 'que' is mandatory. Then: je crois que (I believe), je trouve que (I find). Opinion + any sentence they own.
constructions.watchFor: que + il/elle contracts to qu'il / qu'elle. Reward stacking: opinion + comparison + connector.

constructions.title: I'm hungry → j'ai faim (have, not be)
constructions.goal: Meet the avoir-idioms where French has what English is.
constructions.transferHook: French HAS states English IS: j'ai faim (I have hunger = I'm hungry), j'ai raison (I'm right), j'ai besoin de (I need = have need of). One flip unlocks a family.
constructions.targetPattern: j'ai + faim / soif / raison / besoin de + [X]
constructions.watchFor: 'j'ai besoin de' + infinitive is the power chunk (I need to...). Watch for learners inserting 'suis'.

constructions.title: First, then, so → d'abord, ensuite, donc
constructions.goal: Tell a whole little story in order.
constructions.transferHook: Narrative glue: d'abord (first), ensuite/après (then), donc (so), enfin (finally). Combine with both pasts and the future to narrate like in English.
examples: d'abord j'ai préparé, ensuite j'ai commencé
c'était difficile, donc j'ai décidé de continuer
constructions.watchFor: This is a synthesis node: push for 3-4 linked sentences using only owned material. Length is the win.

constructions.title: Tell me your day
constructions.goal: Capstone: narrate real life mixing every owned system.
constructions.transferHook: No new grammar — the transfer is confidence: everything needed to describe a real day already exists in their inventory (pasts, future, opinions, connectors, quantities).
constructions.targetPattern: Free narration: 5+ sentences about a real or imagined day.
examples: hier je suis allé au bureau, il y avait beaucoup de travail...
demain je vais organiser mon projet parce que c'est important
constructions.watchFor: Resist teaching. Only prompt with questions (et ensuite ? pourquoi ?) and let them build. Mastery = a connected multi-sentence narration.
